hints: Trace the exact journey of oxygen on paper: alveolar air space, into and out of the alveolar wall cell, into and out of the capillary wall cell, then into the red blood cell.
Remember each cell surface membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, so crossing one full membrane means passing through 2 phospholipid layers. Count membranes first, then multiply by 2.
walkthrough:
**Map the journey**

Think like an oxygen molecule. You start in the air in the alveolus and you need to get to haemoglobin inside a red blood cell in the capillary.

To do that you must go right through two thin cells in the walls, then into the red cell.

**Count the membranes crossed**

You go into and out of each wall cell, but only into the red cell because haemoglobin is free in its cytoplasm.

That is: into alveolar epithelial cell (1), out of it (2), into capillary endothelial cell (3), out of it (4), into red blood cell (5). So 5 membranes in total.

**Convert membranes to phospholipid layers**

This is the key trick. One plasma membrane = one bilayer = 2 layers of phospholipids.

Calculation:
$$5 \text{ membranes} \times 2 \text{ layers per membrane} = 10 \text{ layers}$$

options.A: 4 layers is only 2 membranes. That would miss most of the journey through the alveolar wall, capillary wall and red cell.
options.B: 6 layers is only 3 membranes. This undercounts, as you must enter and leave two wall cells plus enter the red cell.
options.C: 8 layers is only 4 membranes. This is a common slip where students forget the final entry into the red blood cell membrane.
options.D: 10 layers is correct for 5 membranes: in and out of alveolar cell (4), in and out of endothelial cell (4 more), plus into red cell (2 more).
